title.en: Distinguish electron-pair geometry from molecular shape

summary: Distinguish ideal electron-domain geometry from molecular shape and separately sourced distorted atomic positions.
objective: Build molecular geometry that explains why a shape is bent or pyramidal rather than asserting it.
applies_when: A molecule with lone pairs on the central atom is displayed.
Bond angles are labelled or compared between molecules.
The scene explains polarity, shape or why similar formulas look different.
example_prompts: Compare methane, ammonia and water and explain the angle differences.
Show the lone pairs and the resulting shape.
negative_signals: Predicting or replacing experimental atomic coordinates from the ideal-domain model; sourced measured geometry may instead be shown as a distinct comparison.
not_for: Predicting or replacing experimental atomic coordinates from the ideal-domain model; sourced measured geometry may instead be shown as a distinct comparison.

principles: The electron-pair geometry around a central atom is not the same as its molecular structure: the first counts all regions of electron density, the second describes only where the atoms are.

Quote ideal angles with their domain pairs: linear 180 degrees, trigonal planar 120, tetrahedral approximately 109.5, trigonal bipyramidal 90 for axial-equatorial pairs, 120 for equatorial pairs and 180 for the opposite axial pair; octahedral adjacent pairs are 90 and opposite pairs180 degrees.

Lone pairs explain deviations, case by case rather than uniformly. Because a lone pair occupies a larger region of space than a bonding pair, the source reports the ammonia HNH angle as slightly smaller than 109.5 degrees; that is an example, not a rule that every remaining angle shrinks. Which angles change, and by how much, depends on the geometry and needs its own evidence or measured data.
Showing only the atoms hides the cause, and showing only the domains hides what the molecule is; a good scene lets the viewer see both.
implementation: For an ideal-domain illustration, place domains from their count and identify bonding versus lone-pair sites. For a sourced distorted molecular geometry, preserve the supplied atomic coordinates and show the ideal-domain construction as a separately identified comparison.
Label the electron-pair geometry and the molecular shape as two separate readouts so the distinction is explicit.

State whether displayed angles are ideal values from the domain geometry or measured values from a data source, name the two domains each angle spans, and keep the ideal-domain diagram and any separately sourced distorted atomic positions as distinct views rather than one blended picture.
Let the viewer toggle lone-pair visibility to see the same molecule as domains and as atoms.
When comparing molecules, keep the central atom and orientation aligned so the angle differences are the visible difference.
observable_checks: In ideal-domain views within the same domain family, compare the shared ideal domain arrangement and the different subsets occupied by atoms. Check sourced distorted atomic coordinates against their own data; do not require them to coincide with ideal domain sites.
Measure the modelled angles and confirm they match the stated ideal or sourced values rather than an arbitrary placement.
Confirm the labels for electron-pair geometry and molecular shape are both present and not interchanged.
Toggle lone pairs and confirm nothing else in the geometry moves.

creative_affordances: Lone pairs can be shown as lobes, clouds or ghosted domains; the representation is a design choice.
An abstract domain-only view is a valid companion to the atomic view.
known_limits: Authored modelling guidance citing the predictive model and its ideal angles; real measured geometries differ and require structural data.
It does not cover hypervalent exceptions, resonance or computational chemistry results.

claims.statement: Electron-pair geometry describes all regions of electron density around a central atom, while molecular structure describes atom positions. Ideal angles are 180 degrees for linear, 120 for trigonal planar and approximately 109.5 for tetrahedral arrangements. In trigonal bipyramidal geometry axial-equatorial pairs are 90 degrees, equatorial pairs 120 and the two opposite axial domains 180; octahedral adjacent and opposite pairs are 90 and 180 respectively. The ammonia HNH angle is slightly smaller than 109.5 degrees because its lone pair occupies more space than a bonding pair.
claims.scope: Ideal VSEPR domain geometries and the source ammonia example. Pair-specific angles describe the ideal construction, not measured experimental geometries or a universal direction of lone-pair distortion.
